item.title: Estate agency’s debt problem is getting harder to ignore
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK’s estate agency sector is facing mounting financial challenges as rising interest rates and declining property sales put pressure on heavily indebted firms. With inflation reaching 3.5% in September, the Bank of England increased the base rate to 4%, signalling potential further hikes. At the same time, agreed property sales are 8% lower than the same period last year, according to Rightmove. This combination of higher borrowing costs and reduced income is creating a difficult environment for estate agency groups carrying significant debt.

The Impact of Rising Finance Costs

Many estate agency groups have expanded through acquisitions, often financed by substantial borrowing. However, the cost of servicing this debt is becoming increasingly burdensome. For example, Leaders Romans Group, owned by Hadrian Holding Limited, reported a 15% increase in revenue to £298.8 million in 2025. Despite this growth, the group faced annual finance costs of £50.7 million, exceeding its adjusted EBITDA. This resulted in a pre-tax loss of £69.5 million, with bank borrowings rising to £418.7 million. Some of its loan facilities carry interest rates above 11%, reflecting the steep cost of debt in the current economic climate.

Similarly, Lomond, formerly under Chianti Holdings Limited, reported a £32.1 million loss on turnover of £116.6 million in 2024, with interest costs matching the loss figure. Although the group has since been refinanced under new ownership, the substantial cost of financing its earlier expansion highlights the risks associated with aggressive growth strategies.

Growth Ambitions vs Financial Reality

Despite these challenges, some estate agencies continue to pursue ambitious growth plans. Dwelly, backed by Prospire Technologies Ltd, has completed 13 acquisitions this year, increasing its managed property portfolio to over 16,000. The business has secured significant investment and debt financing to support its target of managing 50,000 properties by the end of 2026. However, its 2025 accounts revealed a £3.7 million loss, raising questions about the sustainability of its strategy.

In contrast, Connells, owned by Skipton Building Society, has taken a more cautious approach. After completing 13 acquisitions in 2025, the group has paused further purchases during 2026, with plans to resume in 2027. Its chief executive described this decision as an opportunity to “fix the roof,” suggesting a focus on stabilising finances before pursuing additional growth.

As the estate agency sector navigates these challenges, firms may need to reassess their strategies to balance growth ambitions with financial stability. With borrowing costs remaining high and property sales under pressure, a cautious approach could prove prudent in the current climate.

item.title: Rightmove’s dominance faces growing test as housing market weakens, analysts warn
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Rightmove, the UK’s leading property portal, continues to demonstrate resilience amidst a weakening housing market, though analysts caution that its dominance may face growing challenges. Whilst the platform has reported declines in buyer demand and agreed sales, it remains on track to achieve revenue and profit growth this year. However, concerns are emerging about how long it can outperform a market increasingly strained by falling transactions and rising borrowing costs.

Rightmove’s Market Position Under Scrutiny

Despite a 10% drop in buyer demand and a 9% fall in sales agreed, Rightmove has adjusted its revenue growth forecast slightly, lowering the upper end from 8% to 7%. This move has prompted analysts to question whether the portal’s strong market position can shield it indefinitely from broader property market pressures. Rightmove’s dominance in the UK property sector remains a significant advantage, but its ability to monetise this position could be tested if market conditions continue to deteriorate.

Mark Crouch, market analyst at eToro, highlighted that Rightmove’s influence has limits, particularly when buyers and sellers struggle to agree on property values. “The recent interest rate hike adds further affordability challenges for buyers, while sellers remain hesitant to accept lower prices,” he explained. Crouch also noted that estate agents’ reliance on Rightmove could help sustain its income, even as transactions decline. “Estate agents still need to attract buyers, making the platform difficult to ignore,” he said. However, he warned that prolonged market weakness could eventually impact the businesses that fund Rightmove’s success.

Divided Opinions on Future Growth

Analysts are split on Rightmove’s ability to maintain its growth trajectory. Anthony Codling, managing director of equity research at RBC Capital Markets, offered a more optimistic view, suggesting that Rightmove remains relatively insulated from the challenges facing estate agents. He pointed to the portal’s strong competitive position and its ability to adapt to changing market conditions as key factors supporting its resilience.

Conversely, others argue that sustained market stagnation could undermine Rightmove’s dominance. Falling buyer demand, fewer agreed sales, and pressure on housebuilders could eventually squeeze the estate agents and developers who pay to advertise on the platform. Whilst Rightmove’s resilience has been notable, the longer the UK’s property market remains in stalemate, the harder it may become for the portal to monetise its position effectively.

As the housing market navigates ongoing challenges, homeowners and property professionals may wish to monitor how platforms like Rightmove adapt to evolving conditions. Whilst its dominance remains intact for now, the portal’s ability to sustain growth in a weakening market could prove pivotal in the months ahead.

item.title: Renters’ Rights Act already shutting out good tenants, letting agent warns
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The Renters’ Rights Act, introduced earlier this year, has reportedly made it more challenging for certain groups of tenants to secure rental properties. According to industry experts, landlords have become increasingly cautious about who they accept, particularly favouring applicants with straightforward financial profiles. This shift has left international students, self-employed individuals, and business owners facing additional hurdles, even when they have substantial savings or alternative income streams.

Impact on Tenants with Non-Traditional Finances

Prior to the Renters’ Rights Act reforms in May 2026, tenants could offer six or twelve months’ rent upfront to secure a property. This practice was particularly common among international students and those without a UK-based income or guarantor. However, the new legislation prohibits landlords from requiring large advance payments as a condition of tenancy. Whilst tenants can still choose to pay rent early after moving in, landlords can no longer insist on this upfront, leading to greater caution in their selection process.

Mo Kanso, managing director of London-based letting agency Landstones, highlighted that tenants with unconventional financial arrangements, such as those relying on investments, dividends, or irregular payments, are increasingly finding it difficult to meet referencing requirements. “Someone might not have a £100,000 PAYE salary paid monthly, but they could have significant savings or receive substantial dividends throughout the year,” Kanso explained. Despite their financial stability, these tenants are often overlooked in favour of those with regular UK salaries.

Growing Reliance on Guarantor Services

As landlords become more selective, many tenants are turning to professional guarantor companies to improve their chances of securing a rental property. These firms provide landlords with added security, ensuring rent payments are covered if the tenant defaults. However, this service comes at a cost, with some tenants quoted fees equivalent to several weeks’ rent.

Kanso noted that while guarantor services offer a solution, they can place an additional financial burden on tenants. “Landlords are increasingly reluctant to take risks, especially when tenants lack conventional references or a suitable guarantor,” he said. This cautious approach has led to a growing reliance on these services, particularly among international students and self-employed individuals.

The Renters’ Rights Act was designed to create a fairer rental market, but it appears to have inadvertently introduced challenges for certain groups of tenants. For those affected, exploring alternatives such as guarantor services or providing additional financial documentation could help improve their chances of securing a property.

item.title: Landlords reverse plans to sell as falling house prices change the sums
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Many landlords in the UK are reportedly reconsidering their plans to sell their properties, as falling house prices and strong tenant demand make retaining rental investments a more appealing option. This shift comes despite increasing tax and regulatory pressures, with some investors opting to remain in the private rented sector rather than risk selling at a loss.

Why landlords are rethinking their exit strategies

According to estate agency Virelle Group, which operates in London, Manchester, and Birmingham, sluggish property sales and declining apartment values have led landlords to pause their exit plans. Selling in the current market could result in significant financial losses, making it less attractive for investors to offload their portfolios. Additionally, the impending Renters’ Rights Act and changes to rental income taxation, set to take effect in April 2027, have added further complexity to the decision-making process.

Emily Robison, director at Virelle Group, highlighted that many landlords are choosing to hold onto their properties rather than sell. She explained, “The sales market has remained sluggish, and apartment values have fallen significantly, which would see the majority of landlords make a loss if they sold up.” This trend is particularly pronounced in London, where research from Chestertons suggests that one in four landlords who had marketed their properties for sale have since returned them to the rental market.

Opportunities for landlords who stay

The departure of some landlords from the market has created opportunities for those who choose to remain. With fewer rental properties available, demand from tenants has strengthened, potentially leading to higher rental yields. Robison noted, “The Renters’ Rights Act and looming tax changes convinced a considerable number of private landlords to sell their properties this year. This has resulted in a supply shortage of homes for rent, creating an opportunity for remaining landlords.”

Rightmove’s Rental Trends Tracker supports this outlook, showing annual asking rent growth of 2.4% outside London. Meanwhile, rental supply remains under pressure across the UK, further bolstering the case for landlords to retain their investments.

As the property market continues to evolve, landlords may wish to carefully weigh their options before deciding whether to sell or hold onto their portfolios. With falling house prices and strong tenant demand, staying in the rental market could prove financially beneficial for some investors.

item.title: Estate agents face another year of falling prime house prices, Savills warns
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The prime property market in the UK is set to face further challenges in the coming years, according to recent forecasts from Savills. The estate agency predicts that prime house prices will continue to decline in 2027, with some areas experiencing drops of up to 3.5%. This downturn is attributed to a combination of elevated mortgage rates, higher taxes, and ongoing economic uncertainty, which are collectively dampening buyer demand.

Regional Variations in Price Declines

Savills’ forecasts highlight significant regional differences in the expected price declines. Prime central London is anticipated to see a modest drop of 2%, while outer prime London could experience a steeper fall of 2.5%. Across prime regional markets, values are also expected to decrease by 2%. The outlook is particularly challenging for London’s suburbs and commuter belts, where buyers remain highly sensitive to borrowing costs. Additionally, weaker demand from those relocating out of the capital is contributing to the pressure on prices in these areas.

Long-Term Recovery Prospects

Despite the near-term challenges, Savills suggests that a gradual recovery is on the horizon, albeit at varying rates across different regions. The agency expects most prime markets to return to growth by 2028, driven by lower mortgage rates and improving economic conditions. However, prime central London may not see price increases until 2029. Over the five-year period to 2031, prime regional values are forecast to rise by 11.9%, compared to 9.7% in outer prime London and 8.7% in prime central London.

Frances McDonald, director of residential research at Savills, emphasised the difficult conditions faced by buyers and sellers in the prime property market. “Owners and buyers continue to grapple with elevated borrowing costs, tax and political uncertainty, and heightened price sensitivity,” she noted. “As a result, the recovery is likely to take longer than previously expected, with values remaining under pressure across most markets during 2027.”

Five-Year Growth Forecasts

Savills’ detailed forecasts provide insights into the expected performance of various prime markets over the next five years. For instance, London suburbs are predicted to see a 7.5% increase in values by 2031, while the Midlands and North could experience a more robust growth of 14.7%. Scotland and Wales are also expected to perform well, with projected increases of 17.0% and 15.3%, respectively. These forecasts relate to average second-hand property values, rather than new-build homes.

Whilst the prime property market faces a prolonged period of adjustment, Savills maintains that it is “down, not out.” Prospective buyers might consider adopting a medium- or long-term perspective, as the market is expected to stabilise and grow from 2028 onwards. For those navigating the current uncertainties, staying informed about regional trends and seeking professional advice could be beneficial.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Two recent appointments in the UK property industry highlight the movement of experienced professionals into new roles, bringing fresh expertise to their respective markets. From London to Chester, these changes reflect the evolving landscape of estate agency and property management.

Knight Frank Welcomes New Head of Fulham Sales

Knight Frank has appointed Tom Roper as the head of sales for its Fulham office, marking a significant addition to its team. Roper brings over 12 years of experience in London’s residential property market, having previously served as a senior sales branch director at Kinleigh Folkard & Hayward (KFH). Before his tenure at KFH, he honed his skills at Countrywide, establishing himself as a seasoned professional in the sector.

In his new role, Roper will lead the Fulham sales team, collaborating with Knight Frank’s regional partners and broader London network. Reflecting on his appointment, Roper expressed enthusiasm for joining Knight Frank, citing the firm’s esteemed reputation and client-focused approach. He also highlighted his deep knowledge of the Fulham market and his commitment to delivering exceptional results for clients.

Luke Ellwood, regional partner at Knight Frank, praised Roper’s track record of leading successful sales teams in South West London. Ellwood expressed confidence that Roper would strengthen the firm’s presence in Parsons Green and drive further growth.

Chester Estate Agent Continues Family Legacy

In Chester, Anna Horne has stepped into a prominent role within the local property industry by joining the committee of the Chester Association of Property Professionals (CAPP). Horne, a sales negotiator at Cavendish, follows in the footsteps of her father, Alex Horne, who is a former chairman of CAPP and a well-known figure in Chester’s property sector.

Her appointment comes as David Adams, Cavendish’s managing director, steps down after 16 years of service on the committee. Founded in 1949, CAPP plays a vital role in supporting local property professionals by offering continuing professional development (CPD), networking opportunities, and industry events.

Horne joins a committee that includes her colleague Annie O’Brien, Cavendish’s lettings development manager, who serves as membership secretary. This new chapter for Horne underscores the importance of family legacy and continuity within the property industry.

These appointments demonstrate the dynamic nature of the UK property market, with experienced professionals stepping into roles that leverage their expertise and passion. Homeowners and industry observers alike may find these developments encouraging as they reflect a commitment to excellence and innovation in the sector.

item.title: Surveying skills shortage threatens housing delivery – RICS
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK’s surveying sector is facing mounting challenges as skills shortages and a lack of preparedness for technological advancements threaten its ability to support housing and infrastructure development. According to the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS), these issues are placing significant strain on the profession, with many firms struggling to meet rising demand.

Skills Shortages Impacting Capacity

The RICS Surveying Skills Report – UK Snapshot, published in November 2026, highlights that skills shortages are having a critical or moderate impact on 50% of UK organisations. Over 60% of respondents reported reduced capacity to meet client demand, raising concerns about the industry’s ability to support ambitious housebuilding and infrastructure projects.

Recruitment challenges are particularly acute, with 62% of respondents citing a lack of mid-career and experienced surveyors as the biggest issue. Additionally, 47% identified shortages of graduates and early-career professionals, while 43% mentioned staff retention as a growing concern. These gaps are also affecting workforce development, with 55% of firms stating they lack sufficient time or resources to train existing employees effectively.

The AI Skills Gap

While technology, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), could help alleviate some of these pressures, the report reveals a significant gap in the profession’s readiness to embrace it. Nearly 60% of surveyors feel unprepared or only slightly prepared to work with generative AI, AI analytics, and AI-driven workflows. In contrast, just 12% consider themselves well or very well prepared.

Despite this, 30% of respondents identified AI, automation, and digital tools as key strategies for addressing future skills shortages. James Garner, head of AI and data at Gleeds, emphasised the importance of integrating AI training into surveying education. “AI must become a core, formally assessed part of surveying education. The profession’s future depends on it,” he said. Garner also criticised universities that discourage AI use rather than teaching students how to apply the technology responsibly.

However, the report underscores that traditional professional skills remain essential. Communication, collaboration, and stakeholder management were ranked among the most important skills for the future, alongside technological proficiency.

Broader Implications for the Property Market

The survey’s findings have broader implications for the UK property market and infrastructure development. With firms struggling to recruit and retain skilled professionals, there is a risk that delivery timelines could be delayed, potentially impacting housing supply and economic growth. Addressing these challenges will require a concerted effort from industry leaders, educational institutions, and policymakers to ensure the sector is equipped to meet future demands.

As the surveying profession navigates these pressures, adopting a balanced approach that combines technological innovation with the development of traditional skills could be key to overcoming current and future challenges.

item.title: Conveyancing fees fall again as competition squeezes firms’ margins
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Conveyancing fees in the UK have continued to decline, with the latest figures revealing a 3% drop in the third quarter of 2026. This downward trend comes amidst increasing competition among conveyancing firms and a challenging housing market. According to data from Reallymoving, the average cost for a combined property sale and purchase now stands at £2,365, including VAT, expenses, and disbursements. This represents a £73 decrease from the previous quarter and a 3.5% fall compared to the same period last year.

Declining Fees Amid Market Challenges

The conveyancing industry is facing a complex set of pressures, with fees falling whilst operational costs rise. After adjusting for inflation, conveyancing costs dropped by 3.9% quarter-on-quarter and 6.5% year-on-year. This decline is partly attributed to subdued activity in the housing market, which has intensified competition among firms. Homeowners may find this trend beneficial, as it could reduce the overall cost of moving. However, for conveyancers, it presents a significant challenge, particularly when coupled with rising compliance demands and workforce shortages.

Reallymoving’s analysis of over 77,000 conveyancing quotes highlights further details. The average cost of purchasing a property fell from £1,509 in Q2 to £1,479 in Q3, whilst selling costs decreased from £929 to £887 over the same period. These reductions, whilst modest, reflect the broader trend of falling fees across the industry.

Workforce Pressures and Recruitment Efforts

The conveyancing sector is grappling with a shortage of qualified professionals, adding to the strain on firms. The Council for Licensed Conveyancers (CLC) recently launched a major recruitment campaign, Project 2,000 Lawyers, aimed at attracting 2,000 additional trainees to qualify as licensed conveyancers by 2030. This initiative comes in response to a significant decline in the number of authorised practitioners, which has fallen from 13,000 in 2021 to around 10,000 today.

Workforce shortages could potentially undermine efforts to speed up property transactions and reduce delays, which are already a concern for many homebuyers and sellers. Additionally, conveyancing firms are contending with increasingly complex regulatory requirements, including anti-money laundering obligations, building safety responsibilities, and the growing threat of cybercrime.

Regional Variations in Conveyancing Costs

The decline in conveyancing fees has been widespread, with nine of the UK’s 12 regions recording reductions in Q3. The West Midlands saw the sharpest fall, with fees dropping by 9.3%, followed by the East Midlands at 5.3% and Northern Ireland at 5.2%. Only three regions experienced slight increases: the East of England (0.3%), the South West (0.2%), and Wales (0.2%). Despite these increases, these regions remain relatively affordable compared to London, where the average cost for a combined sale and purchase remains the highest at £2,975.

Whilst falling fees may benefit homeowners, they add pressure on conveyancing firms to maintain profitability whilst investing in compliance, technology, and workforce development. This balancing act is becoming increasingly difficult in a competitive and challenging market environment.

For those considering a property move, it could be worth exploring conveyancing quotes to take advantage of the current downward trend in fees. However, homeowners might also wish to consider the broader challenges facing the industry, which could impact service levels and transaction times.

item.title: Britain’s most affordable towns revealed
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

New research from Zoopla has revealed a striking regional divide in housing affordability across Britain, with Scotland and the North East dominating the list of the most affordable locations. The analysis, which examined 929 towns, found that property prices in 36 towns are less than twice the combined annual earnings of two local full-time workers. This highlights the growing gap between northern and southern property markets, particularly as higher mortgage costs continue to impact buyers’ purchasing power.

North East and Scotland Lead in Affordability

County Durham claims the top three spots in Zoopla’s affordability rankings, with Shildon leading the way. The typical property in Shildon is valued at just £73,600, equivalent to 1.15 times the combined annual earnings of two local workers. Ferryhill and Peterlee follow closely behind, with average home prices of £91,500 and £96,500 respectively. These three towns are the only ones out of the 929 analysed where typical property values fall below £100,000.

Scotland also features prominently, accounting for 23 of the 36 most affordable towns. Fraserburgh, for example, has a typical property value of £116,000, which is 1.59 times local household earnings. Meanwhile, Workington in the North West and Ferndale in Wales represent their regions as the most affordable towns, with average home prices of £114,900 and £116,200 respectively.

The Affordability Gap in the South

In stark contrast, southern England remains significantly less affordable. The South East is the second least affordable region after London, with the typical home valued at £395,700 – equivalent to 5.33 times household earnings. Even in Dover, the most affordable town in the South East, the average property price stands at £206,300, or 2.97 times local earnings.

London’s affordability challenges are particularly pronounced. Tower Hamlets, the capital’s most affordable borough, has an average property value of £455,200, which is 4.91 times household earnings. This underscores the difficulties faced by buyers in southern regions, where property prices far outstrip local incomes.

Key Takeaways for Buyers

For those looking to purchase a home, the research highlights the importance of considering location when assessing affordability. Borrowers might find better value in northern regions and Scotland, where property prices are more closely aligned with local earnings. However, it’s essential to factor in other costs, such as mortgage rates and living expenses, when making a decision.

With the affordability gap widening, homeowners may wish to explore their options carefully and seek professional advice to navigate the current market. Whilst the North East and Scotland offer attractive opportunities, buyers in the south could face greater challenges in finding affordable properties.

item.title: Propertymark One moves to larger London venue for 2027 conference
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Propertymark has announced that its flagship annual conference, Propertymark One, will be held at a larger venue in London next year. Scheduled for 25 June 2027, the event will take place at the ICC Auditorium in ExCeL London, marking a significant upgrade from previous years. With over 2,000 property professionals expected to attend, the conference aims to provide an even more comprehensive experience for delegates.

Expanding the Event

The move to ExCeL London follows the success of this year’s conference, which attracted nearly 2,000 attendees. The 2027 event will feature two main stages, eight breakout sessions, and over 100 exhibition stands, making it the largest Propertymark One conference to date. The expansion reflects the growing demand for insights and networking opportunities within the property sector. Previous conferences have brought together estate agents, policymakers, and industry leaders, with discussions covering topics such as transaction delays, regulatory reform, and the impact of artificial intelligence on the industry.

Jason Lee, head of commercial at Propertymark, emphasised the importance of the venue upgrade. “Moving into the ICC Auditorium allows us to take the event to another level. With two main stages, eight breakout sessions, and our biggest exhibition yet, we’re creating an experience that brings together the people, expertise, and businesses that make this profession what it is.”

Focus on Key Industry Issues

The 2027 conference will focus on pressing issues affecting the property market, including housing reform, regulatory compliance, and the role of artificial intelligence in driving agency growth. Proposed changes to the home-buying and selling process will be a key topic, alongside evolving material information requirements. For letting agents, sessions will examine legislative changes and their implications for landlords, tenants, and agency operations.

The event will also explore how technology can improve efficiency and help agents meet changing consumer expectations. Propertymark has yet to announce the full speaker line-up for 2027, but it is expected to include representatives from both within and outside the property industry. Previous speakers have included high-profile figures such as deputy prime minister and housing secretary Angela Rayner, who addressed delegates on housing policy and sector challenges.

As the property market continues to evolve, Propertymark One 2027 aims to provide valuable insights and practical solutions for professionals navigating an increasingly complex landscape. With its expanded format and focus on key issues, the conference is set to be a must-attend event for anyone involved in the property sector.

item.title: Landlord law Newsround #461
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent insights into rent tribunals, landlord adaptations to new legislation, and updates on the PRS database have dominated the property news landscape this week. From tribunal decisions to tenant rights, these developments could influence how landlords and tenants navigate the rental market in the coming months.

Rent Tribunal Outcomes analysed

Analysis of rent tribunal cases from September has revealed that only 28.4% of landlords were granted their full requested rent increases. Out of 68 cases, 21 resulted in full increases, 29 saw partial increases, 12 remained unchanged, six were reduced, and another six were dismissed. The average rent increase amounted to £92 per month, rising from £1,372 to £1,464. Cyborg Finance, which conducted the analysis, noted that the £47 tribunal fee might represent good value, given the potential returns. However, the process can take up to four months, with an average delay of 91 days between serving a rent increase notice and receiving a tribunal decision. Landlords seeking to justify rent adjustments might find tools such as market rent guides and tribunal kits helpful in preparing evidence.

Landlords Adapt to the Renters’ Rights Act

Since the Renters’ Rights Act came into effect, landlords have begun adjusting their strategies to comply with the new regulations. A survey by mortgage lender Landbay found that 36% of landlords have increased rents, while 34% have revised their tenant referencing and affordability criteria. Additionally, 16% are now relying more on letting agents or professional bodies for support, and 13% are allocating more funds for maintenance and repairs. Despite these changes, only 17% of landlords are aware of the upcoming landlord registration scheme, with many citing a lack of clarity about its requirements.

PRS Database: Privacy Concerns and Updates

Matthew Pennycook, a government official, recently confirmed that landlords’ details on the new PRS database will remain private until winter 2027. He emphasised that future legislation will determine which records will be made publicly accessible, balancing transparency for tenants with landlords’ privacy rights and data protection concerns. However, the absence of an audit trail has raised some apprehensions. The government has published guidance on registering for the PRS database, which landlords may wish to review to stay informed.

These developments highlight the evolving landscape of the UK rental market, with implications for both landlords and tenants. Staying updated on tribunal outcomes, legislative changes, and database requirements could help stakeholders navigate these shifts effectively.

item.title: 5 Important Costs to Consider Before Buying a Home in New Jersey
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Purchasing a property is a significant milestone, but it’s essential to consider all the associated costs beyond the purchase price. From stamp duty to ongoing maintenance, understanding these expenses can help potential buyers budget effectively and avoid unexpected financial surprises.

Stamp Duty Land Tax

One of the most substantial upfront costs when buying a property in the UK is Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT). The amount payable depends on the property’s purchase price, whether it’s a primary residence or a second home, and if the buyer is a first-time purchaser. For example, first-time buyers in England and Northern Ireland are exempt from SDLT on properties up to £425,000, whilst those purchasing additional properties face higher rates. Buyers may wish to use online SDLT calculators to estimate their liability accurately.

Legal Fees and Conveyancing

Conveyancing, the legal process of transferring property ownership, is another cost to factor in. Solicitors or licensed conveyancers handle tasks such as conducting local searches, reviewing contracts, and registering the property with the Land Registry. Fees can vary depending on the complexity of the transaction and the professional chosen. Additionally, buyers might consider budgeting for local search fees, which cover checks on planning permissions, environmental risks, and other factors affecting the property.

Mortgage Arrangement Fees

For those financing their purchase with a mortgage, arrangement fees are a common expense. These fees cover the cost of setting up the mortgage and can range from a few hundred to several thousand pounds. Some lenders offer the option to add these fees to the mortgage balance, but this could result in paying interest on the amount over the loan term. Borrowers might compare different mortgage deals to find one that balances competitive rates with reasonable fees.

Survey Costs

Before finalising a purchase, it could be worth commissioning a property survey to assess its condition. Surveys range from basic valuations to more comprehensive structural inspections, with costs increasing accordingly. While a basic survey might suffice for newer properties, older homes could benefit from a detailed report to identify potential issues like damp or structural problems. Addressing these early on could save significant repair costs down the line.

Ongoing Maintenance and Running Costs

Owning a property also involves ongoing expenses, such as council tax, utility bills, and maintenance. Homeowners may wish to set aside a budget for regular upkeep, including repairs, gardening, and decorating. Energy efficiency improvements, such as insulation or double glazing, could also reduce utility bills in the long term. Additionally, those living in leasehold properties might need to account for ground rent and service charges.

Understanding these costs can help prospective buyers make informed decisions and ensure they’re financially prepared for homeownership. Thorough research and careful planning are key to navigating the process smoothly and avoiding unexpected expenses.

item.title: Major property firm to close almost half its offices as losses mount
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Vistry, one of the UK’s leading housebuilders, has announced plans to close nearly half of its offices across the country as part of a major restructuring effort. The firm aims to reduce its office network from 25 locations to just 13, with the closures set to take effect in January 2025. This move is expected to save the company £50 million next year but could result in significant job losses among its 4,500-strong workforce. The decision comes amidst mounting financial pressures, including a record half-year loss of £661 million reported in September.

Challenges in the Housing Market

The restructuring reflects broader challenges facing the UK housing market, with higher mortgage rates and weaker buyer demand impacting both developers and homeowners. Vistry has warned that it anticipates building fewer homes in the coming months due to these market conditions. Chief executive Adam Daniels described the decision as "difficult but necessary," emphasising the need to create a "smaller, more focused and disciplined business."

Financial pressures have been exacerbated by rising borrowing costs, with the average five-year fixed mortgage rate climbing to 5.99% in recent months, up from 4.96% in February. This increase has placed additional strain on buyers already grappling with affordability issues. According to Savills, UK house prices are expected to decline in 2027, with a potential recovery not anticipated until the latter half of 2028. Regions such as London, the South East, and the East of England are predicted to face the most significant challenges.

Government Funding and Housing Targets

Despite securing £350 million in government funding in August to support affordable and social housing developments, Vistry’s struggles highlight the broader slowdown in the housing sector. This downturn raises concerns about the government’s ambitious target of delivering 1.5 million new homes in England during this parliamentary term. Official figures indicate that there have been 306,640 housing starts across the UK since July 2024, though this figure does not directly align with the England-specific goal.

The Bank of England’s decision to increase interest rates from 3.75% to 4% has further compounded pressures on the mortgage market, creating additional hurdles for both buyers and developers. Investors have also reacted cautiously to the uncertain economic outlook, adding to the challenges faced by the housing sector.

As Vistry navigates these turbulent times, its restructuring plans underscore the wider difficulties confronting the UK property market. Homeowners and prospective buyers may wish to monitor developments closely, particularly in light of rising mortgage rates and shifting market conditions.

item.title: Lloyds reveals latest UK house price figures as market faces fresh pressure
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

UK house prices experienced their most significant annual decline in three years during October, as rising mortgage rates and economic uncertainty continued to weigh on the property market. According to the latest Lloyds House Price Index, property values dropped by 0.6% in October, bringing the average UK house price to £296,285. This figure also represents a 1.2% year-on-year decrease, marking the steepest annual fall since October 2023. Quarterly data further highlights the slowdown, with prices declining by 0.5%. These trends come amidst weaker buyer demand, fewer sales agreed, and growing affordability pressures.

Economic Pressures Impact Housing Market

item.title: The UK Property Market is dead. Who told the buyers?
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Despite headlines painting a bleak picture of the UK property market, homes are still being bought and sold. Recent data suggests that whilst the market may not be as buoyant as in previous years, it is far from lifeless. The key question is: what do the numbers really tell us about the current state of the housing market?

Understanding the Numbers

In Week 43, there were 27,500 new property listings, slightly down from 30,300 the previous week. This figure is also below the 2026 weekly average of 35,500. However, year-to-date listings stand at 1.529 million, which is marginally lower than 2025’s figure but higher than the averages for 2024, 2023, and the pre-pandemic years.

When it comes to sales, 21,800 homes were sold subject to contract in Week 43, a small dip from 22,100 the week before. Year-to-date sales total 1.032 million, which is 7.5% lower than 2025 but still above the figures for 2023 and the pre-Covid period. Net sales, which account for fall-throughs, also show a similar trend, with 795,000 homes sold year-to-date.

Challenges for Estate Agents

One of the themes emerging from the data is the challenge estate agents face in accurately valuing properties. Overvaluing homes can lead to extended periods on the market, ultimately resulting in price reductions. This not only frustrates homeowners but can also impact the agent’s reputation.

For example, in Weybridge, a closer look at local estate agents reveals significant differences in performance. Some agents achieve higher prices and quicker sales, whilst others rely on high volumes of listings without the results to match. This highlights the importance of choosing the right agent, as their approach can make a substantial difference to the outcome of a sale.

Whilst the headlines may suggest a struggling market, the data tells a more nuanced story. Homes are still selling, and listings remain robust compared to recent years. For those considering a move, it could be worth focusing on the numbers rather than the noise, ensuring informed decisions are made in a complex market.

item.title: Energy efficiency rules are changing: what should landlords do now?
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

With the introduction of the Energy Independence Bill to Parliament earlier this month, landlords across England and Wales may need to prepare for potential changes to energy efficiency regulations in the private rented sector. Whilst the bill covers a wide range of energy-related topics, its implications for rental properties could be significant, particularly regarding compliance and enforcement of minimum standards.

Key Changes for Landlords

The bill, specifically Clause 173, amends the Energy Act 2011, granting the government broader powers to regulate energy efficiency in privately rented properties. One notable change is the potential extension of these regulations to properties occupied under a licence, such as short-term holiday lets, though the government has stated it has no immediate plans to implement this. Additionally, the bill clarifies that "property" includes parts of a property, which could impact Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) where rooms are let individually.

For HMOs, the bill allows for specific regulations on how minimum energy efficiency standards apply, including provisions for tenants requesting energy efficiency improvements. This could mean landlords may need to adapt their properties to meet stricter requirements, particularly in cases where tenants seek upgrades such as insulation or more efficient heating systems.

Enforcement and Compliance

Another significant aspect of the bill is the strengthening of enforcement mechanisms. It introduces provisions for inspections of non-domestic properties to ensure compliance with energy efficiency standards, although this will not apply to residential properties. Additionally, energy efficiency assessments carried out to demonstrate compliance may, in certain circumstances, be treated as a relevant improvement themselves. This could streamline the process for landlords, ensuring their properties meet the necessary standards without requiring multiple assessments.

Landlords might also need to consider how these changes could affect their bottom line. Whilst improving energy efficiency could lead to lower utility costs and increased property value, the upfront costs of upgrades could be substantial. However, with the government’s focus on sustainability, there may be opportunities for grants or incentives to offset these expenses.

What Should Landlords Do Now?

Whilst the bill has yet to become law, landlords may wish to start preparing for potential changes. Reviewing the energy efficiency of their properties could be a proactive step, particularly for those with HMOs or properties that may fall under the expanded scope of regulations. Staying informed about future developments, including any new regulations or government schemes, could also help landlords remain compliant and avoid potential penalties.

Ultimately, the Energy Independence Bill signals a shift towards greater emphasis on energy efficiency in the private rented sector. By taking early action, landlords can position themselves to meet these evolving standards whilst potentially enhancing the appeal and value of their properties.

item.title: BREAKING: Property industry reacts to Bank of England interest rate hike
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Bank of England has announced its first interest rate rise in over three years, increasing the base rate from 3.75% to 4%. This decision, made by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), comes amidst ongoing inflationary pressures, largely driven by rising energy and oil prices. Whilst the increase was widely anticipated, it has sparked concerns about its potential impact on mortgage borrowers and the wider housing market.

What Does This Mean for Mortgage Borrowers?

Homeowners with tracker mortgages, which are directly linked to the Bank of England base rate, will see an immediate increase in their monthly repayments. Those on variable-rate mortgages may also face higher costs, depending on their lender’s terms. However, borrowers on fixed-rate deals will remain unaffected until their current term expires. That said, homeowners approaching the end of their fixed-rate period might find themselves facing higher borrowing costs when they remortgage.

Lenders may have already factored in this rate rise when pricing fixed-rate mortgage products, but the possibility of further increases could keep mortgage rates elevated. This uncertainty could pose challenges for prospective buyers and those looking to remortgage in the near future.

Why Did the Bank of England Raise Rates?

The decision to raise interest rates was driven by persistent inflationary pressures. The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rose to 3.5% in September, the highest level in 11 months and significantly above the Bank’s 2% target. Rising global oil prices, exacerbated by geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, have been a key factor in pushing inflation higher.

Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey emphasised that the rate increase should not be seen as the start of a prolonged cycle of hikes. However, he warned that further increases could follow unless progress is made towards resolving geopolitical conflicts, particularly in the Middle East. Bailey stated that future decisions would depend on developments in energy prices and inflation dynamics.

Whilst the Bank’s move aims to curb inflation, it comes at a delicate time for the housing market. Buyer confidence remains fragile, and housing transactions are already under pressure. Estate agents and property professionals are likely to feel the impact of higher borrowing costs, which could dampen market activity further.

For homeowners and buyers, staying informed about market trends and seeking professional mortgage advice could help navigate these uncertain times. With the potential for further rate rises on the horizon, careful planning and budgeting may be essential for those approaching remortgaging or entering the property market.

item.title: Estate agents brace for fresh mortgage blow as Bank of England rate decision looms
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The Bank of England’s latest interest rate decision, due to be announced today, could have significant implications for the UK housing market and mortgage borrowers. With the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) widely expected to raise the Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4%, homeowners and prospective buyers may face increased financial pressures. This potential rise, the first since August 2023, comes amidst ongoing concerns about inflation and its impact on mortgage affordability.

Impact on mortgage borrowers

A quarter-point increase in the Bank Rate would have an immediate effect on homeowners with tracker mortgages, as these are directly linked to the Bank Rate. Borrowers on other variable-rate deals could also see their monthly repayments rise. Those on fixed-rate mortgages would be shielded from any immediate changes, but homeowners approaching remortgage might face higher costs if lenders adjust their rates in response to the Bank’s decision.

Mortgage pricing is heavily influenced by swap rates, which reflect market expectations of future borrowing costs. As such, lenders may have already factored in today’s anticipated rate rise. However, the Bank’s commentary on future rate increases could prove equally significant. Any suggestion that borrowing costs will remain elevated for an extended period could further dampen buyer confidence and limit affordability.

Housing market outlook

The potential rate rise coincides with a cautious outlook for the UK housing market. Recent data from HMRC shows a 1% decline in residential transactions in September, with activity down 4% compared to the same period last year. This slowdown reflects the broader impact of rising mortgage costs on purchasing power and sales activity.

Forecasts from Savills add to the uncertainty, predicting a 1.5% drop in UK house prices in 2027. The estate agency anticipates a broadly flat market in 2026, with property values remaining around 3% below their recent peak. Savills has also revised its expectations for a sustained recovery, now predicting this is unlikely to occur before the second half of 2028. The firm does not expect average mortgage rates to fall below 5% until early 2028, assuming the Bank Rate will peak at 4.25% by the end of 2027 before declining to 3.25% in 2028.

Emily Williams, director of residential research at Savills, highlighted the impact of global events on the housing market, noting that ongoing conflicts and economic instability could prolong the period of uncertainty for buyers and sellers alike.

As the Bank of England prepares to announce its decision, homeowners and prospective buyers may wish to carefully assess their financial position and explore their options. With mortgage costs and market conditions in flux, staying informed and seeking professional advice could help navigate the challenges ahead.

item.title: Rent arrears surge 50% in wake of Renters’ Rights Act
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

New data reveals a significant rise in rent arrears across the UK, with nearly one in five tenancies now experiencing missed or outstanding payments. According to figures from Reposit, a deposit alternative provider, 18% of tenancies fell into arrears during the third quarter of 2026, marking a 50% increase compared to the same period in 2025. This upward trend has raised concerns for landlords and letting agents, as 2026 is on track to record the highest arrears rate in three years.

Rising Housing Costs Strain Tenants

The surge in rent arrears coincides with escalating housing costs for tenants. Despite a slowdown in rental inflation, the average UK private rent reached £1,406 per month in September 2026, reflecting a 3.8% annual increase. This equates to an additional £52 per month for tenants. Meanwhile, wage growth has struggled to keep pace, with regular earnings rising by just 3.7% in the three months to August. Private sector pay increased by 3%, whilst inflation stood at 3.5% in September, further squeezing household budgets.

Although more tenancies are falling behind on payments, the average amount owed has remained relatively stable. Reposit reports that the average debt stands at £1,837, only £13 higher than the previous year. However, this figure still exceeds the average five-week cash deposit of £1,258 by £579, leaving landlords with greater financial exposure.

Landlords Face Increased Risks Under New Legislation

The rise in arrears comes as landlords adapt to the Renters’ Rights Act, which came into effect in England in May 2026. The legislation abolished Section 21 no-fault evictions and introduced stricter processes for landlords seeking possession of their properties. This has made it more challenging for landlords to address unpaid rent and regain control of their assets.

Ben Grech, chief executive of Reposit, highlighted the growing financial risks for landlords. He noted that traditional tenancy deposits, averaging £1,258, now fall significantly short of the average arrears amount of £1,837. "With the Renters’ Rights Act making it harder for landlords to regain possession, the financial risk associated with tenant arrears has become a bigger concern than ever before," he said.

Ministry of Justice figures also show a 6% year-on-year increase in landlord possession claims in England and Wales during the second quarter of 2026, with courts receiving 23,635 claims. However, these figures encompass various possession grounds, not solely rent arrears.

As tenants grapple with rising rents and landlords navigate the complexities of new legislation, both parties face mounting challenges in the UK’s rental market. For landlords, understanding the financial risks and exploring alternative protection measures could be essential in safeguarding their investments.

item.title: Upfront property information could unlock faster offers, survey suggests
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

A recent survey by LRG suggests that providing upfront property information could significantly influence buyers’ decisions and potentially speed up the homebuying process. The research found that over 80% of prospective buyers would be more inclined to make an offer if they had access to key details such as surveys, legal packs, and chain information ahead of time. This shift towards greater transparency could reshape how properties are marketed and sold in the UK.

Boosting Confidence and Speed

The survey highlights that upfront information does more than just accelerate transactions—it also builds buyer confidence. Among respondents, 41% said they would feel more assured about making an offer with this information readily available, while another 41% indicated they would be likely to act sooner. Families looking to upsize were particularly influenced, with 48% stating they would offer more quickly and 36% gaining greater confidence in their decision.

For buyers moving to similarly sized homes, reassurance appeared to be a priority. Over half (51%) said upfront details would increase their confidence, whilst 30% noted it would encourage them to proceed faster. These findings suggest that transparency could help address some of the uncertainties that often delay or derail property transactions.

Government Reforms and Industry Initiatives

The survey aligns with recent government proposals to streamline the homebuying process. In June, ministers announced plans to introduce upfront sales packs, which could reduce transaction times by approximately four weeks and halve the number of failed sales. LRG has also launched its own initiative to provide property information earlier, joining a growing trend in the industry.

Ryan Mathews, group managing director of surveying at LRG, emphasised the dual benefits of upfront information. “Whilst it’s often discussed as a way to speed up sales, it also gives buyers greater confidence in the offers they are making,” he said. “Surveys, in particular, provide crucial reassurance by helping buyers understand the property’s condition and any issues that may need attention.”

Challenges and Considerations

Despite the potential advantages, there are challenges to consider. Seller-commissioned surveys, while helpful, raise questions about their scope, accuracy, and reliability for prospective buyers. Mathews highlighted the importance of ensuring buyers fully understand what these reports cover and how current they are. Early identification of potential issues could reduce the risk of renegotiations later in the process, but clarity and trust in the information provided remain key.

As the industry continues to explore ways to improve transparency, it could be worth considering how upfront information is presented and verified. Buyers and sellers alike may benefit from clearer guidelines and standards to ensure the process is both efficient and reliable.

In conclusion, providing upfront property information appears to offer significant benefits, from boosting buyer confidence to potentially speeding up transactions. However, addressing concerns around accuracy and liability will be crucial to making this approach a success in the long term.
